blocks.text: Church, Israel was camped on the plains of Moab, and Balak the king of Moab was scared to death of them. So he sent for a man named Balaam, who was known for speaking blessings and curses. Balak offered him a big reward to come and curse God's people.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: God had told Balaam plainly not to curse the people he had blessed. Then God let him go with the king's men, on one condition. He could only say what God gave him to say.

verses.text: And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with the princes of Moab.

verses.text: And God’s anger was kindled because he went: and the angel of the LORD stood in the way for an adversary against him. Now he was riding upon his ass, and his two servants were with him.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: Three times that donkey saved his life, and three times he beat her for it. He was so set on where he was going, he never once asked why she would not go.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: Later on, when Balaam stood on the hills over Israel's camp, he opened his mouth to curse them for the king. And every single time, blessing came out instead. God would not let his people be cursed.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: Now that story is funny, and it is supposed to be. A famous man who claimed he could see what others could not was out-seen by his own donkey. Sometimes the thing blocking your road is not against you, Church. It might be the mercy of God, standing in the way.

first_reader.note: Written by Claude in the landing session, then Claude's pastor and cultural read.

pastor.note: Faithful to Num 22:21-35; the angel of the LORD read only by the narrator; set-up and blessings (22:1-20, 23-24) told without invented speech.

cultural.note: 'God is in the way' at the turn; humour aimed at pride, never at any people.
